Select, sort and filter records with SQL
Aggregate and combine tables with joins
Keep data clean and create your own tables

questions.q: When we use a database, what does the database manager do?
options: It designs the tables for us
It is a program that manipulates the database for us
It stores a backup copy of the data
questions.explain: Queries are sent to a database manager — a program that manipulates the database on our behalf.
questions.evidence: a program that manipulates the database for us

questions.q: Records in a table are not stored in any particular order. How do you show them in a specific order?
options: Specify the order explicitly with ORDER BY
Rows always come back in the order they were inserted
questions.explain: Ordering is never implicit: you must ask for it with ORDER BY.
questions.evidence: if we want to display them in some order, we must specify that explicitly with ORDER BY

questions.q: Which clause specifies the conditions a record must meet to be included in a query's results?
questions.explain: WHERE filters records; SELECT then decides which columns to show.
questions.evidence: Use WHERE to specify conditions that records must meet in order to be included in a query's results.

questions.q: Which keyword combines the results of two or more queries into one result set?
questions.explain: UNION stacks the results of several queries; JOIN combines columns from several tables.
questions.evidence: Use UNION to combine the results of two or more queries.

questions.q: A record's test in WHERE evaluates to null. What happens to that record?
options: The query stops with an error
It is left out — WHERE keeps only records for which the test is true
questions.explain: Null is neither true nor false, and WHERE keeps only rows whose test is true.
questions.evidence: the only records kept by a WHERE are those for which the test is true

questions.q: If you add two values and one of them is null, what is the result?
questions.explain: Null means 'unknown', so arithmetic with it is unknown too.
questions.evidence: If we add two values, and one of them is null, the result is null.

options: A value, or combination of values, that uniquely identifies each record in a table
A value from one table that identifies a record in another table
The first column of every table
A password that protects the database
questions.explain: A primary key identifies each record uniquely; a foreign key points at another table's records.
questions.evidence: A primary key is a value, or combination of values, that uniquely identifies each record in a table.

questions.q: A value from one table that identifies a unique record in another table is called a…
questions.explain: Foreign keys are what joins match on.
questions.evidence: A foreign key is a value (or combination of values) from one table that identifies a unique record in another table.

questions.q: Why should every value in a database be atomic?
options: So a value doesn't contain parts we might want to work with separately
Atomic values use less disk space
Because SQL cannot store long text
questions.explain: Store parts separately (for example family and personal names) instead of splitting strings later.
questions.evidence: not contain parts that we might want to work with separately

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is it simpler and safer to modify data?
options: When the table has no columns
When you have just deleted the table
When every record has a unique primary key
questions.explain: A unique key lets you target exactly the record you mean to change or delete.
questions.evidence: It is simpler and safer to modify data when every record has a unique primary key.
